summary: Defines an X.509 certificate extension that lets a certificate list the S/MIME capabilities of its owner, complementing the S/MIME Capabilities attribute in signed messages. It gives an optional way to say which cryptographic algorithms an entity supports. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This extension lets an X.509 public-key certificate state which S/MIME capabilities its subject supports. A sender can use that information when choosing encryption, but remains responsible for choosing sufficiently strong protection.

questions: what is the s/mime capabilities certificate extension
how does a certificate list encryption capabilities
when should an application use smime capabilities
subtitle: An X.509 certificate extension for stating an entity's S/MIME capabilities.

tldr.problem: A sender may need to choose encryption for a recipient without knowing the recipient's S/MIME capabilities from earlier exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an optional X.509 certificate extension that carries the same SMIMECapabilities structure used in signed S/MIME messages.
tldr.outcome: Applications may use the certificate's capability information, but should prefer more reliable and relevant authenticated information when available.

today: RFC 4262 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Capability Information Before a Message Exchange
sections.content:
S/MIME messages can report a sender's cryptographic capabilities in a signed message attribute. But a sender may need to encrypt a message before any recent exchange has revealed the recipient's capabilities. In that case, the sender otherwise has to rely on out-of-band information or defaults, which may not fit the recipient's capabilities or security policy.

This RFC defines an optional extension in the recipient's X.509 public-key certificate to provide that information in advance. The extension is static: the asserted capabilities remain unchanged until the certificate expires or is revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender may need to encrypt a message before learning what algorithms the recipient supports. The recipient's certificate can provide that information ahead of time.

sections.title: The S/MIME Capabilities Extension
sections.content:
The extension uses the same data structure as the SMIMECapabilities attribute defined for S/MIME messages. It can include different kinds of S/MIME capabilities, with the intended purpose mainly being to identify content-encryption algorithms. Certification authorities SHOULD limit included capabilities to those relevant to the certificate's intended use.

The extension MUST NOT be marked critical. Applications MAY ignore capabilities and SHOULD gracefully ignore ones that are not relevant to the certificate's use.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate extension uses the existing S/MIME capability format. It is optional information, and applications can ignore capabilities that do not apply.

sections.title: Using and Updating the Information
sections.content:
An application SHOULD NOT use this extension when more reliable and relevant authenticated capability information is available. Because the extension records capabilities at certificate issuance, implementers should consider changes during the certificate's lifetime. A change may require revocation if a listed algorithm is considered broken or too weak for the governing security policy.

The RFC emphasizes that the sender remains responsible for choosing encryption strong enough to protect the information.
sections.plainLanguage: The listed abilities may become outdated while a certificate is still valid. Senders must still choose encryption strong enough for the information they send.
